core: The Atlantic World as an interconnected system created by European colonization of the Americas from the 16th century onward
The Columbian Exchange: transfer of crops, animals, and diseases between the Americas, Europe, and Africa after 1492
The demographic catastrophe among Indigenous Americans from Old World diseases and European conquest
The transatlantic slave trade: an estimated ~12.5 million enslaved Africans embarked (1501-1866), of whom roughly 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage, per the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database
The triangular trade and the plantation economies (sugar, tobacco, cotton) built on enslaved forced labor
Enslaved people's humanity, agency, resistance, and culture
The lasting consequences for Africa, the Americas, and Europe, and the abolition timeline
supporting: Spanish conquest of the Aztec (Tenochtitlan, 1521) and Inca (1530s) empires
Main African embarkation regions (West Central Africa, Bight of Biafra, Gold Coast, Senegambia) and American destinations (Brazil, Caribbean, mainland North America)
Mercantilism as the economic logic of Atlantic empire
outOfScope: The voyages of exploration themselves (owned by history:foundations:exploration; referenced only)
U.S. domestic slavery as an institution (owned by history:foundations:slavery)
Pre-contact African kingdoms in depth (owned by history:foundations:african-kingdoms)

claims.claim: After 1492 the Columbian Exchange moved American crops (maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, tobacco, manioc) to the Old World and Old World crops and livestock (wheat, sugarcane, horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, chickens) to the Americas, transforming diets and economies on both sides of the Atlantic.

Old World infectious diseases such as smallpox, measles, typhus, and influenza killed Indigenous Americans who had no acquired immunity at catastrophic rates, estimated by some scholars as high as 95 percent in affected populations; OpenStax gives a pre-contact Indigenous population of roughly seventy-five million around 1492.

Spanish conquistadors overthrew large Indigenous states: Hernan Cortes captured Moctezuma II in 1519 and Tenochtitlan fell after a siege in 1521, and Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire between 1530 and 1533, executing the ruler Atahualpa.

The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (SlaveVoyages) estimates that about 12.5 million enslaved Africans (12,521,337) were embarked from Africa between 1501 and 1866, of whom roughly 10.7 million disembarked alive in the Americas, meaning more than 1.8 million people died during the Middle Passage.

By the database's estimates, Brazil received the largest number of disembarked captives (about 5.85 million) and the British Caribbean the second largest (about 3.26 million), while mainland North America received about 554,000, a small fraction (roughly 4-5 percent) of the total.

The 'triangular trade' linked three legs: European manufactured goods and firearms shipped to West Africa and exchanged for captives; the Middle Passage carrying enslaved Africans to the Americas; and plantation commodities such as sugar, tobacco, and cotton shipped back to Europe.

Sugar was the most valuable and labor-intensive plantation crop of the Atlantic economy, alongside tobacco, rice, indigo, coffee, and later cotton; most enslaved people were forced to labor on sugar plantations in the Caribbean and Brazil.

Enslaved Africans were human beings who exercised agency: on the Middle Passage some refused food or leapt overboard rather than submit, and in the Americas enslaved people resisted through sabotage, flight, and armed revolt while sustaining music, foodways, and religion.

Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 and slavery across most of its empire in 1833; the United States banned the importation of enslaved people from 1808; and Brazil, the last country in the Americas to do so, abolished slavery in 1888, consistent with the trade's estimated end date of 1866 in the database.

positions: SlaveVoyages: ~12.5 million embarked minus ~10.7 million disembarked implies more than 1.8 million deaths at sea.
OpenStax rounds to roughly 12 million transported with about 2 million dying during voyages.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the precise figures (12.5M / 10.7M / >1.8M) to the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database and dates them, treating the OpenStax rounding as consistent corroboration rather than a competing count.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only boilerplate ('Atlantic World is a foundational concept in History...') with no substantive historical claims; all of it was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the placeholder definition of 'Atlantic World' with the historical concept of the interconnected Atlantic system (Columbian Exchange, colonization, slave trade).

sourceRecords.title: World History, Volume 2, from 1400 - 5.4 The Atlantic Slave Trade
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-20. Supports: the triangular trade (manufactured goods to Africa, captives across the Middle Passage, American commodities to Europe); ~12 million Africans transported late 1400s-early 1800s with roughly 2 million dying on the voyages; by the 1700s about 61,330 crossing per year, ~42% to the Caribbean and ~38% to Brazil; sugar as the most valuable, labor-intensive crop, plus tobacco, rice, indigo, coffee; Middle Passage conditions (500-600 people per ship, 10-20% mortality); resistance (refusing food, jumping overboard, sabotage, revolt) and cultural survival (music, food, religion). CC BY; original synthesis, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Britain and the Trade / Slavery education resource
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-20. Supports: more than 11 million enslaved people transported across the Atlantic over 300 years with Britain a leading carrier from the mid-17th century; the three-legged triangular trade (British manufactured goods and firearms to West Africa, the Middle Passage, and slave-produced sugar, cotton, and tobacco back to Britain); Parliament's 1807 Act for the Abolition of the Slave Trade and the 1833 abolition of slavery in British territories; the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron. Government source used as reference; figures attributed, no prose reproduced.
